features: A SPLIT ACROSS TWO TABLES IS NO LONGER LOST — No migration: the database is not touched. An expense item split across two millesimal tables lost the second one every time its edit card was opened and saved.

THIS IS NOT AN EXOTIC CASE, IT IS THE TEXTBOOK ONE. Article 1126 of the Italian civil code splits the cost of a roof terrace in two: one third to whoever has exclusive use of it, two thirds to everyone else. In KondoManager you do this by linking two millesimal tables to the same item, each with its weight. The same applies to article 1124 on stairs and to lifts.

WHAT HAPPENED: the edit card for an item knows only one table — it reads the first and sends that one. On save, the program deleted every other link and their allocations. Opening the card to correct an amount, or a name, was enough to halve the split. Without asking anything, and without saying anything.

THE DAMAGE WAS NOT A WRONG CHARGE, and the credit goes to beta.63: when the coefficients declare only part of the cost, the allocation records the remainder as uncovered — a visible line, with its own reason. So nobody silently paid someone else's share. What was lost was the data, and the work to rebuild it.

NOW THE SAVE LEAVES IT ALONE, AND THE CARD SAYS SO. On an item split across several tables the table selector no longer appears — showing one out of two would be worse, because it would present a split that is not the real one — and in its place it says how many tables the item is divided across, that name, amount and notes can still be edited, and that the split itself is changed from the linked tables section.

WHY THE FIX STOPS HERE: teaching that card to handle several tables is a new screen, that is, a feature, and it belongs in 1.11. What could not stay in 1.10 is a screen destroying data it cannot even display. It is the same principle already written into the program for converting an item into a chapter, which demands an explicit confirmation before removing linked tables: never a silent deletion inferred from a save.

UNDER THE BONNET: five new checks, three of them counter-checks — that the amount and name still save (a guard satisfied by refusing the save would be worse than the defect), that an item with a single table still behaves exactly as before, and that the scenario under test really is the two-table one and not something that has since changed.
